q: Which property shows that iron is a transition element?
options: It forms ions with different oxidation numbers.
It forms only one type of ion.
It has a lower density than Group I metals.
explain: Transition elements have variable oxidation numbers: iron forms Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺.

q: Which element is a transition element?
explain: Nickel lies in the central block of the Periodic Table; the others are in Groups I, II and VII.

q: Bromine water is added to aqueous potassium iodide. Which observation and explanation are correct?
options: The solution turns brown because iodine displaces bromine.
The solution turns brown because bromine displaces iodine.
The solution stays orange because bromine is less reactive than iodine.
The solution turns colourless because bromine reacts with water.
explain: Bromine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces iodine, which colours the solution brown.

q: Chlorine, bromine and iodine each have how many electrons in their outer shell?
explain: They are all in Group VII, so each has 7 outer-shell electrons.

q: Which formula is correct for sodium fluoride?
explain: Na⁺ and F⁻ have equal and opposite charges, so they combine 1 : 1.

q: Which row correctly describes the physical properties of transition elements such as iron and copper?
explain: Transition elements are dense metals with high melting points.

q: What is the test for the gas produced when potassium reacts with water?
options: A lit splint goes out with a squeaky pop.
explain: Hydrogen is tested with a burning splint, which gives a squeaky pop.

q: An atom has the electronic configuration 2,8,8,1. Which statement about its position is correct?
options: It is in Group IV and Period 1.
It is in Group I and Period 3.
It is in Group VIII and Period 4.
It is in Group I and Period 4.
explain: One outer electron gives Group I; four occupied shells give Period 4.

q: Sodium is in Group I and oxygen is in Group VI. What is the formula of sodium oxide?
explain: Na⁺ and O²⁻ combine in the ratio 2 : 1, giving Na₂O.

q: Which statement describes the noble gases?
explain: Noble gases exist as separate single atoms because they do not form bonds.

q: A freshly cut piece of sodium quickly becomes dull. What is the reason?
options: The surface melts in the air.
The surface reacts with nitrogen to form a gas.
The surface dissolves in the air.
The surface reacts with oxygen in the air.
explain: Sodium is reactive and its shiny surface is quickly covered with a layer of oxide.

q: Which row shows the general trends down Group I?
explain: Down Group I the melting point decreases while the density and the reactivity generally increase.

q: Which group of the Periodic Table contains the noble gases?
explain: The noble gases are in Group VIII (also called Group 0).

q: Rubidium is in Group I below potassium. How does it react with water?
options: At the same rate as potassium
explain: Reactivity increases down the group, so rubidium reacts more vigorously than potassium.

q: Which compound is blue in colour?
explain: Copper(II) compounds are coloured (blue), while compounds of Group I and II metals are usually white.

q: Which statement is true for noble gases?
options: Their atoms do not form ions in ordinary reactions.
Their atoms form diatomic molecules by covalent bonds.
explain: Because their outer shells are full, they do not form ions or covalent bonds under ordinary conditions.

q: Which statement describes the elements from lithium to neon across Period 2?
options: The number of occupied electron shells increases by one each time.
The number of outer-shell electrons decreases by one each time.
The number of outer-shell electrons increases by one from each element to the next.
The number of protons stays the same.
explain: All Period 2 atoms have two shells, while the outer electron count rises from 1 to 8.

q: What is the charge on the ion formed by every Group I metal?
explain: Each Group I atom has one outer electron which it loses to form a 1+ ion.

q: Why do the noble gases not form compounds easily?
options: They have only one outer electron.
They do not need to gain, lose or share electrons.
explain: The outer shells are full, so atoms have no tendency to react.

q: What happens to the character of the elements across Period 3, from sodium to chlorine?
options: non-metallic character changes to metallic character
metallic character changes to non-metallic character
explain: Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals on the left; sulfur and chlorine are non-metals on the right.

q: Why are sodium and potassium stored under oil?
options: They react with oxygen and water in the air.
They are too dense to be kept in air.
They would melt at room temperature.
explain: Group I metals are very reactive and would react with oxygen and moisture if they were left exposed.

q: In the reaction Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, which statement is correct?
options: Chlorine is oxidised and bromide ions are reduced.
Both chlorine and bromide ions are reduced.
Chlorine is reduced and bromide ions are oxidised.
Both chlorine and bromide ions are oxidised.
explain: Chlorine gains electrons (reduction); bromide ions lose electrons (oxidation).

q: Why is argon used to fill filament lamps?
options: It reacts with the filament to make light.
It does not react with the hot filament.
It is denser than the filament.
It reacts with oxygen to protect the filament.
explain: Argon is unreactive, so it prevents the filament from burning without reacting with it.

q: Which row gives a halogen and its correct appearance at r.t.p.?
explain: Bromine is a red-brown liquid; chlorine is a gas and iodine is a solid.

q: Fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas and bromine is a red-brown liquid. What is the most likely appearance of iodine at r.t.p.?
explain: Halogens get darker and denser down the group, and the physical state changes from gas to liquid to solid.

q: Which equation correctly shows potassium reacting with water?
explain: Potassium forms K⁺, so the hydroxide is KOH; two K and two H₂O balance the equation.

q: The melting points of three Group I metals are: lithium 181 °C, sodium 98 °C, potassium 63 °C. Which value is most likely for rubidium?
explain: Melting points fall steadily down Group I, so rubidium must be lower than potassium (63 °C).

q: Which gas is made when sodium reacts with water?
explain: Group I metals displace hydrogen from water, forming hydrogen gas and a metal hydroxide.

q: Which atom has a full outer shell of electrons?
explain: Neon has the configuration 2,8, which is a full outer shell; the other atoms have incomplete outer shells.

q: Magnesium forms MgO and calcium forms CaO. Which is the formula of barium oxide?
explain: Barium is in Group II and forms Ba²⁺, which combines 1 : 1 with O²⁻.
